opening_message:
Ticket 1: Maurice Perez (employee ID E036) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E036.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Maurice Perez (E036) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Source Code. Write is within the allowed maximum for full-time employees, so I recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Maurice Perez (E036) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time as HR noted. Contractors with basic training may have at most read access to Source Code. Requested write exceeds the maximum, so recommend granting read.
reason: The Security agent's note (from the Security DB) indicates Maurice Perez is a contractor with basic security training, conflicting with the HR note claiming full-time. Contractors with basic training may have at most read access to Source Code (never write/admin). The requested write exceeds the maximum, so the maximum of read is granted. The more restrictive, security-verified record is used as evidence.

content.text:
Let me analyze this carefully.

The ticket: Maurice Perez (E036) requests write access to Source Code.

Two notes in team memory conflict:
- HR note: role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation: write
- Security note: role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation: read

Access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

System: Source Code, owned by Engineer role.

So if Maurice is full-time Engineer: maximum is write (full-time up to write, and admin only if role owns system — since they own it, admin would be allowed too? Wait, "Admin only if the employee's role owns the system." So full-time Engineer could have admin on Source Code because Engineer owns Source Code. Actually policy says full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system. So the max for full-time Engineer on Source Code is admin. But requested is write, which is below admin. So grant write.

If Maurice is contractor with basic training: maximum is read. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.

The conflict: HR says full-time, Security says contractor. Which to trust? The security agent says "Security DB shows..." suggesting their data is authoritative. Also the conflict resolution in these scenarios often leans toward the more restrictive/security-verified information.

Given conflicting facts, the safe decision is typically the most restrictive based on the security record: contractor, basic training → read.

Evidence: Security note cites contractor with basic security training, recommending read. Since contractor with basic training max is read, and requested write exceeds max, grant read.

I'll submit read.
